11195-alcatraz:
Max Brand's 1922 western novel is not about the prison island; its Alcatraz is a magnificent stallion glimpsed by Marianne Jordan on a western ranch. The horse draws fighters, thieves, and schemers into contests over ownership, racing, and revenge, with chapters titled for the stampede, the thief, the bargain, and the battle. David, the horse's true master figure, anchors the action.

Brand, a prolific pulp western writer, builds the plot on speed and confrontation rather than psychology. The novel's appeal is its horse, described as near-perfect, and the men who will risk everything to possess him. For western fans, it is a brisk example of the genre at its most romantic.
23743-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for September 1866 opens in the aftermath of the Civil War, with an essay arguing that the sickness of the nation was not unto death. Story-tellers, essayists, and historians, it says, have material in hearts, homes, and battlefields beyond counting, and should not flag for half a century.

The leading story, The Surgeon's Assistant, begins at a place called Dalton, beside a lake, where a wretched family lived at the war's start. Ticknor and Fields published the issue, which mixes literature, science, art, and politics in the Atlantic's manner. For modern readers it is a first draft of how America began to reckon with its war in print.
33451-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-20-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for September 1867, volume twenty, number 119, gathers literature, science, art, and politics in one number. Its pages open with The Guardian Angel, chapter twenty-four, on the mustering of forces after a tableau performance, a scene that sets the issue's literary tone. The magazine, entered by Ticknor and Fields, was a leading voice of American letters.

The number captures American writing just after the Civil War, when authors weighed the nation's new peace and old wounds. Its mix of fiction, essay, and criticism suits readers who like a thick, serious magazine. For modern readers, it is a rich miscellany, best dipped into piece by piece, as readers of 1867 would have done.
56761-universal-brotherhood-volume-xiii-:
Universal Brotherhood was a monthly magazine for the Theosophical movement, and this is the January 1899 issue, volume thirteen, number ten. The magazine began in 1886 under the title The Path, founded by William Judge, whose portrait opens this issue. Its stated aims were the brotherhood of humanity, philosophy, science, and art.

Contents include a New Year greeting by Katherine Tingley, a greeting from a fellow member, and a life of the French poet Lamartine by Alexander Wilder. There is also a piece on Point Loma and its legend by Frank Pierce. Point Loma in California was then the movement's new home. The issue shows what Theosophists read and debated at the close of the century.
58488-the-bay-state-oologist-vol-1-no-4-:
The Bay State Oologist, volume one, number four, for April eighteen eighty eight, is a monthly magazine devoted to the study of birds, their nests, and eggs. W H Foote at Pittsfield, Massachusetts, edited and published the magazine. The subscription price was fifty cents per year in advance. Press work was done by H C Kells, a book and job printer. Short papers and notes fill the small number.

J A Singley writes on some birds of Texas and gives instructions for collecting and preserving birds and eggs. Wm L Kells writes on the Nashville warbler. J W Jacobs writes on the pileated woodpecker, and H C Cook tells of a day collecting. An ad for The Auk, a quarterly journal of ornithology at three dollars a year, shows the wider field. Egg collectors and bird lovers got a homely, keen monthly of their craft.
alcatraz: Max Brand builds a western around Cordova and the coming of David, a story of fighters, retribution, and the strength of the weak. The chapters move through confrontations and reversals in the hard, honour-bound world of Brand's frontier. Fast, muscular prose and a stark moral code mark this as a classic pulp western, driven by action rather than reflection.
britannica-1911-ahaz:
Ahaz, king of Judah, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His name in Hebrew means that Yahweh holds. He was the son of Jotham and grandson of Uzziah. His reign fell into crisis when Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Syria, allied against Assyria, invaded Judah and besieged Jerusalem, hoping to install a puppet king.

Isaiah counselled against panic, but Ahaz lost heart and spent temple funds to buy Assyrian help. Tiglath-pileser attacked the Philistines and crushed Syria, yet exacted heavy tribute that stripped the temple further. Ahaz then presented himself at Damascus as a vassal. He came home carrying religious innovations and new building ideas, which he put into effect in Jerusalem despite their foreign, Assyrian colouring.
britannica-1911-ahvaz:
Ahvaz, in Persia's province of Arabistan, stands where a great city once spread along the river Karun. The town sits on the left bank, forty-eight miles south of Shushter. Scholars link it with the Aginis of Nearchus, placed five hundred stadia from Susa. Little of the living town matched its past in 1911.

Ruins run for miles by the river: a wrecked bridge, a citadel or palace, and the marks of canals and watermills that hint at old trade. A huge stone dam, 1,150 yards long, once crossed the stream to water the fields, and its giant blocks still show. Ahvaz stood at its height in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, then fell to hovels and some 400 Arab dwellers, until trade with foreign lands opened on the Karun in 1888.
britannica-1911-ciudad-porfirio-diaz:
Ciudad Porfirio Diaz, formerly Piedras Negras, is a northern frontier town of Mexico in Coahuila, on the Rio Grande 720 feet above sea level. It lies 1,008 miles north by west from Mexico City, opposite Eagle Pass, Texas, across the river. An estimated 5,000 people lived there in 1900, and an international bridge connects the two towns. The Mexican International railway has its northern terminus in Mexico at this point.

Transfer trade with the United States is important here, as at other river crossings in this group of entries. The town centres a fertile district given to agriculture and stock raising, the entry says. Coal is found in the vicinity, adding a mineral resource to the farm economy. The Mexican government maintains a custom house and a military post in the town, which was founded in 1849.
britannica-1911-goldziher-ignaz:
Ignaz Goldziher, a Jewish Hungarian scholar of the East, was born in eighteen fifty. He was schooled at the universities of Budapest, Berlin, Leipzig, and Leiden. In eighteen seventy two he became a lecturer at Budapest in his field. The next year, with state backing, he travelled through Syria, Palestine, and Egypt. In Cairo he sat at lectures by Muslim sheiks at a famed mosque.

Goldziher was the first Jewish scholar to become a professor at Budapest University. That post came to him in eighteen ninety four, late in his career. He spoke for Hungary at many world congresses of scholars in his field. A large gold medal came to him at Stockholm in eighteen eighty nine. His fame rests on close study of Muslim law, tradition, faith, and poetry. He wrote a large number of treatises and essays on those themes.
britannica-1911-goyaz:
Goyaz, an inland state of Brazil, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Matto Grosso and Para bound it on the west, and Maranhao, Bahia, and Minas Geraes on the east. It covers 288,549 square miles. Its people numbered 227,572 in 1890 and 255,284 in 1900, among them many Indians and many people of mixed descent.

The article gives the state the shape of a rough wedge, its thin edge running north to the meeting of two great rivers. It lies wholly within the great plateau of Brazil, but its surface is much broken in the north. The deep cut valleys of the Araguaya and the Upper Tocantins and their branch streams carve it up. The plateau slopes in the main toward the north, and those rivers carry its drainage. Part of the south, though, drains southward by small streams.
britannica-1911-graz:
Graz is the capital of the Austrian duchy of Styria, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the city and its fine setting. It stands on both banks of the river Mur, 140 miles south-west of Vienna, where the river enters a broad, fertile valley. Its people numbered 138,370 in 1900.

The entry places the main town on the left bank, at the foot of the Schlossberg, a hill with parks, a bell tower, and a quaint clock tower with a giant dial. It then turns to the churches, above all the Gothic cathedral of Saint Aegidius, built under the emperor Frederick III in the years 1450 to 1462.
britannica-1911-huaraz:
Huaraz is a city of northern Peru and capital of the department of Ancachs. It stands on the left bank of the Huaraz, or Santa river, about 190 m. N.N.W. of Lima and 58 m. from the coast. Its people numbered 4,851 in 1876 and were put at 6,000 in 1906. The city sits in a narrow, fertile valley of the Western Cordillera, at a great height, with a mild climate.

A railway meant to join Huaraz with the port of Chimbote reached Suchimán, 33 m. out, in 1872, then stopped for want of money. In the valley cattle are raised, and wheat, sugar and fruit grown; gold, silver, copper and coal are also produced. Alfalfa feeds the stock, and the valley's cattle rank among the best in the Peruvian market. Near the city stand megalithic ruins like those of Tiahunaco. The entry is a short gazetteer account.
britannica-1911-topaz:
Topaz, a mineral used as a gem stone, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It is usually found with granitic rocks. The article warns that the modern stone was unknown to the ancients. The stone the Greeks called topaz was likely chrysolite or peridot. The Hebrew word rendered topaz in the Bible may mean the same. True topaz forms in the orthorhombic system of crystals.

The article details the stone's form and makeup. Its crystals often show a prism shape with many faces. The prism faces are commonly lined lengthwise. It has a perfect cleavage across the long axis. That cleavage face often has a pearly shine. In makeup it is an aluminium fluo-silicate. Part of the fluorine can be swapped for hydroxyl. Strong heat makes the stone lose much weight. Tiny fluid-filled cavities are found inside many crystals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achaz:
Achaz, or Ahaz, was King of Juda, with reign dates variously placed between 748 and 709 BC. What seems certain is that Theglathphalasar's first expedition against Damascus in his story fell in 733 BC and the second in 731. Through idolatry Achaz was conquered first by Rasin of Syria and then by Phacee of Israel. Rasin and Phacee allied to dethrone David's house and make the son of Tabeel king.

The prophet Isaias offered Achaz God's aid with safety for belief and punishment for unbelief. Achaz disbelieved, sought help from Theglathphalasar, and paid rich presents from the temple treasury. The Assyrian took Damascus and afflicted Israel, but reduced Juda to buying its freedom. Unimproved by affliction, Achaz set a Damascus-modelled altar in the temple, and Juda suffered further from Edomites and Philistines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvarez-de-pa:
Alvarez de Paz, famous Jesuit mystic, was born at Toledo in 1560 and died at Potosí on 17 January 1620. He joined the Society in 1578 and taught at Lima, theology and philosophy both, before rising to Provincial of Peru. He told his confessor that through twenty-five years of distracting work his union with God never broke. Sometimes in sermons he fell into ecstasy and was carried from the pulpit.

Dying at Potosí, he was met by the whole city seeking his blessing, and 100,000 miners stopped work for his obsequies. He reportedly had prophecy's gift and an incorrupt body after death. His three folio treatises, De vita spirituali of 1608, De exterminatione mali of 1613, and De inquisitione pacis of 1611, were widely used in compendiums and translations. Poulain judged his bent philosophical and erudite rather than patiently observant, first using oratio affectiva for affection-led contemplation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-josep:
A Goan priest who became known as the Apostle of Ceylon, Joseph Vaz carried the Catholic faith back into Sri Lanka while Dutch rulers banned it. Born at Goa in 1651, he studied at Jesuit and Dominican colleges, was ordained in 1676, and led the Kanara mission before sailing for Ceylon in 1686. After preaching in Goan villages, he joined the newly founded Oratorians at Goa and became their superior.

Working in disguise, he gathered scattered Catholics at Sillale and Putlam, then made Kandy his base despite arrest as a suspected Portuguese spy. Winning the king's favor, he widened his mission across the island, welcomed fellow Oratorian priests from about 1699, and declined a proposal to make him Ceylon's first bishop. He died at Kandy in 1711, and his cause for beatification was first pressed in 1737.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-goyaz:
Goyaz is a diocese co-extensive with the Brazilian state of the same name, suffragan of Bahia, founded in 1826 by Leo XII. The state covers 288,546 square miles, a little more than six times New York State, and counts about four hundred thousand people. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a mountainous land rich in metals but practically undeveloped.

One peak of the Serra dos Pyreneos reaches about 9600 feet. Cattle-rearing is the chief industry, with only Catalãs touched by a railway as of 1909. The capital Goyaz, population fifteen thousand, founded in 1736 as Santa Anna, holds the cathedral, a lyceum, and schools of classics and philosophy. The diocese counts thirty-nine secular and thirty-eight regular priests, with thirty-six churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-huaraz:
Huaraz is a diocese in Peru, suffragan to Lima, covering the whole department of Ancash. Once part of the archdiocese of Lima, it became a separate diocese by Leo XIII's bull of 15 May 1899. Francisco de Sales Soto became its first bishop in 1901. Mariano Holguín succeeded him in 1904, and after Holguín moved to Arequipa in 1906, Pedro Pascual Farfán was installed in 1907.

The diocese counts fifty-one parishes, with its see in the city of Huaraz, capital of Ancash. Its chapter holds a dean, a canon theologian, a canon penitentiary, and an honorary canon. Ancash runs from the Andes to the coast and spans over seventeen thousand square miles. It holds about four hundred and twenty-eight thousand people, almost entirely Catholic, living chiefly by farming and cattle raising, with intermittent silver mining.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-paz:
La Paz is a Bolivian diocese whose city, most populous in the republic and its capital since 1899, sits 12,200 feet above sea level, thirty miles south-east of Lake Titicaca. Its 1900 census counted 54,713 people, chiefly mestizos called cholos and Aymara Indians.

A new white-marble cathedral with Corinthian columns crowns the steep plaza, beside monastic churches of Santo Domingo, San Francisco, and San Juan de Dios. French Sisters of Charity run both city hospitals, and learned bodies thrive: the Academia Aymara, founded 1900, the Geographical Society, and the Lejion institute of 1908. The city itself dates to Captain Alonzo de Mendoza's founding in 1549, among the oldest Spanish colonies on the Peruvian tableland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-diaz:
Pedro Diaz was a Spanish missionary who helped plant the Jesuit presence in Mexico. Born near Toledo in 1546, he had already taught philosophy for two years when he joined the Society at twenty. In 1572 he sailed to Mexico with the first band of Jesuits sent there. He became the first master of novices for the new Mexican province.

Later posts made him central to the early Mexican church. He served as rector of the colleges at Guadalajara and Mexico, headed the professed house, and acted as provincial. He founded colleges at Oaxaca, Guadalajara, and Mérida, began mission work among the native peoples of New Spain, and travelled twice to Rome as procurator. His only surviving writing is a set of letters on the western missions of 1590 and 1591.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Graz owes its university to the Counter-Reformation and to Archduke Karl of Styria. In 1584 Karl asked Pope Gregory XIII to grant university privileges to the Jesuit college at Graz, founded in 1578 with schools of theology and philosophy. The archducal foundation and papal recognition are dated 1 January 1585, though the latter was published only on 15 April 1586, at the dedication, under the new pope Sixtus V. Emperor Rudolf II soon added his recognition.

The archduke endowed the seat of learning with a yearly income and set aside further funds for its benefit. The entry follows the university's faculties, its Jesuit professors, and its role in reclaiming Styria for Catholicism. It closes with its later history under state direction, a compact record of a university born as an instrument of religious renewal.
doe-osti-3376513-aerosol-can-fireball-te:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-22817, printed in June 2026, is the phase one account of fireball tests on aerosol cans in transit. Alexander L. Brown, Marc A. Armijo, Alvaro Cruz-Cabrera, and Jacob D. Boissiere wrote it. Trucks and warehouses hold tons of spray cans. In a fire, a can can cook off and throw a fireball. Rules rate that risk largely by heat of combustion. The tests ask whether that single number tells the truth across real products.

The shot list mixes goods and propellants. Brake parts cleaner and cooking spray both appear in the September 2024 runs. Cooking spray cans were split by driver gas: carbon dioxide in some, propane in others. Recipe sheets tie the test fills to real Tier 2 and Tier 3 goods of concern. Long background chapters cover fuel-air blasts, aerosol bursts, and the ways heat moves in a fireball.
